question: Tell me about a time a colleague said something exclusionary. What did you do?

raiseTranscript.text: In my first project, a teammate joked about how 'the non-native speakers slow us down in standups.' I waited until after the meeting and said it came across as exclusionary because it singled out accents instead of focusing on clarity. He apologized and we agreed to slow down or use chat for questions.
What was the outcome for the team?
Standups stayed the same length but two newer teammates started speaking up more. I checked in with them a week later.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time a colleague said something exclusionary. What did you do?
Junior IC on first project; teammate made accent joke in standup
Pulled colleague aside privately, explained impact, suggested chat for questions
Outcome: two teammates spoke up more; checked in later
Quote: 'I waited until after the meeting and said it came across as exclusionary'
Follow-up: How did you decide to speak up? Candidate: 'I remembered feedback from my mentor on addressing small things early'
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. Principle is Diversity, Inclusion & Belonging on the question of handling exclusionary comments. Candidate described noticing an accent joke, addressing it one-on-one, and following up with affected teammates. This shows ownership of their immediate environment and coachability from prior feedback. The action stayed within individual scope yet produced a visible local result. Biggest strength is the private, specific conversation paired with a later check-in rather than public call-out or silence.

I mentioned it to my manager in our next 1:1 but nothing changed so I just moved on.

raiseTranscript.text: On a cross-team project a peer said the design docs from the India office were 'always late and low quality.' I raised it in our next sync, shared anonymized velocity data showing no difference, and proposed we rotate doc reviews across sites. The other lead agreed and we added it to the team charter.
How did you get the other lead on board?
I showed the data first, then asked what problem they were actually seeing. It turned out to be one delayed handoff, not a pattern.

raiseTranscript.text: During a leadership offsite a VP said we should 'stop hiring from certain universities because they produce too many activists.' I asked for the specific performance data behind the view, then commissioned an anonymized hiring and promotion audit across those schools. Results showed no difference; we added a training module for leaders on sourcing bias and tracked offer acceptance rates from those schools for the next two cycles.
What trade-offs did you consider before the audit?
I weighed the risk of surfacing the comment publicly versus quietly fixing the underlying assumption. Quiet data collection won because it avoided defensiveness while still changing the decision.
